label: Learning and earnings in low- and middle-income countries (shared)

rows.label: Adult earnings gain per standard deviation of literacy and numeracy skills held in adult life, low- and middle-income countries (share of earnings)

source.title: Rossiter, Sandefur and Hares, 'Can Better Test Scores Lift Kids Out of Poverty? The Case for Long-Term Tracking of Education RCTs', Center for Global Development blog, 29 April 2025
source.quote: A reasonable expectation for LMICs might be a return of 25–30 percent per SD increase in literacy skills.
source.note: Their review of studies in low- and middle-income countries (Table 2): observational studies average about 25% (Evans and Yuan 2017, 36.5%; Perez-Alvarez 2017, 28.5%; Perez-Alvarez and others 2023, 16% to 30%; Danon and others 2024, Pakistan, 24%), with no causal identification; the strongest causal evidence 'suggests returns of at least 20 percent'. In rich countries Hanushek, Schwerdt, Wiederhold and Woessmann (2015, 'Returns to Skills around the World: Evidence from PIAAC', NBER Working Paper 19762) find 18% per SD of adult numeracy on average, 12% to 28% (the United States). Ours: 20%, below the observational 25% because those estimates also carry family background and schooling; 10% (rich countries' lower returns, more confounding) to 30% (the top of the review's range for LMICs).

rows.explainer: How much more an adult in a low- or middle-income country earns for each standard deviation of reading and maths skill they hold as an adult: 20% (10% to 30%), from the Center for Global Development's review of the studies that link adults' tests to their earnings. It is per SD of skill still there in adult life; a programme's test gain at the end of the programme is first multiplied by the share of it that lasts (next row). Read by every model of ours valuing education in low- and middle-income countries through later earnings; US youth programmes read @youth_programmes.earnings_gain_per_sd_childhood, measured from childhood gains to adult US earnings.

rows.label: Share of a programme's test-score gain still there as skill in adult life

source.title: Andrabi, Das, Khwaja and Zajonc, 'Do Value-Added Estimates Add Value? Accounting for Learning Dynamics', American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 3(3), 2011, pp. 29-54 (World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 5066)
source.quote: This paper illustrates the central role of persistence in estimating and interpreting value-added models of learning.
source.note: In Pakistan's public and private schools they estimate that only a fifth to a half of what children learn carries over from one grade to the next (abstract). Fade-out slows after the first years, and long-run outcomes re-emerge beyond what faded test scores predict (Chetty and others, Quarterly Journal of Economics 2011, Project STAR). Cross-check in the US: Chetty, Friedman and Rockoff (2014) measure 13% higher earnings per SD of a one-year test gain (@youth_programmes.earnings_gain_per_sd_childhood), against 28% per SD of adult numeracy in the US (Hanushek and others 2015, NBER Working Paper 19762), an implied 46% lasting. Ours: 40%, 20% (Andrabi and others' low end, short catch-up programmes) to 70% (foundational reading and maths that later learning builds on).

rows.explainer: How much of the test-score gain a school programme leaves at its end is still there as reading and maths skill when the child is an adult and working: 40% (20% to 70%), our judgment. Test gains fade: in Pakistan only a fifth to a half of a year's learning carries into the next grade; in the US the earnings gain from a good teacher implies about 46% lasting. Multiplied by @education.earnings_gain_per_sd_adult_skills_lmic in every model of ours valuing education in low- and middle-income countries.
